  Financial Institutions support credit-granting decisions using scorecards trained
  on historical data from previously accepted clients. Since rejected applicants are
  typically ignored during training, the resulting models are affected by sample
  selection bias. The leveraging of information from rejected applicants is known
  as Reject Inference (RI). This thesis introduces a dynamic perspective on RI by
  arguing that discrepancies between the expected performance of a scorecard
  (e.g., estimated through cross-validation) and its realized performance over future
  acceptance rounds constitute a valuable learning signal, which I term *surprise*.
  First, the RI problem is formulated within a measure-theoretic framework to make every
  underlying assumption explicit. Second, the central hypothesis is formulated and
  supporting theoretical and empirical evidence is presented. Finally, an actor-critic
  reinforcement learning agent is proposed to exploit the surprise signal.
